Down the hollow to the stream. I circle it, the light is good, and I can see the pebbles in the reeds. I call: ke-wick! and wait for the answer.
Over the stream, up the meadow, past the lane. I circle and dive, feet out, talons ready.

I fly low over the meadow and the stream. I look for the movement of small things, the rustle in the grass, the flash of a mouse or a pebble. I circle the oak and the ash, the hedgerows and the fence. I listen for the call of the barn owl, and I watch the shadows on the ground. I fly until I find something to eat, then I dive. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
The hollow. The meadow. The stream. I fly low, over the grass, between the trees, and back. I do not go far.
To the oak, the ash, the beech. I go where the light is fading and the mice are stirring. I circle the meadow, the stream, the lane. I call, "ke-wick!" and wait for the answer.
The wood, the stream, the meadow. I fly low, over the treetops, then down to the stream where the pebbles are. I call, "ke-wick!" and wait for the answer.

I fly over the meadow, low and slow, my wings making a soft rustle. I look for movement in the grass, the rustle of a mouse, the flicker of a shrew. I call to the meadow, "ke-wick!" and wait for a response. If I hear nothing, I fly to the stream, where the water reflects the sky and the light is soft. I can smell the earth and the dampness, and I know where the voles are. I fly there at dusk, when the light is fading and the night is coming. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Down the hollow, past the stream, through the meadow to the lane. I fly low, with my wings beating fast, and listen for the rustle of mice or the flicker of a pebble. The meadow is my hunting ground, but sometimes I go farther, to the wood behind the lane, where the undergrowth is thick. I can hear the scurrying from far away, and I follow the sound. I fly low over the meadow and the stream, looking for movement. I see the pebbles in the grass, the shrews in the undergrowth, the mice on the edge of the wood. I call to my mate, and we turn together. Hoo-hoo-hooo.

The meadow. I fly low over the grass, the reeds, the stream. I listen for the rustle of a mouse or the flutter of a pebble. The air is still, the light fades. I turn my head, my eyes narrow. I see the dark shapes, the shapes of things moving. I dive. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The meadow beyond the edge is wide and soft. There is a stream running through it, and the pebbles come there. The lane is a narrow path, lit by the moon, and the road is far, with lights and noise. The lane is where the peafowl live, and the road is where the humans go. I do not cross the edge, but I watch from the oak.
A stream. It runs cold and fast, and it is the only one I know. Beyond that, the meadow, and then the road with lights. I do not go there.

A meadow, and then the river. The meadow is all grass and stones, and the river is dark and wide. I can see the lights of the village from the wood, but I do not go there. The river is cold, and the lights are too bright. I stay in my wood, where the owls are.

A meadow. It stretches wide and flat, the grasses whispering in the wind. Beyond that, the farmland. Crops grow in rows, and the lights of the houses blink like fireflies. Sometimes I hear the hum of tractors and the whine of machinery. But I do not go there. My wood is my world. The meadow is a place of danger, where the dogs run and the men with torches search for me. I stay in my wood,

A field of grass, and beyond that, the river. The river is dark and wide, and it runs cold. I do not cross it. The meadow is full of mice and voles, but they are not as easy to catch as the ones in the wood. The road goes through the meadow, and it is full of lights and noise. I do not like the road. The lane is quieter, but it is where the dogs are. I do not like the dogs.
A stream. The river. The meadow. The lane. The barn. The road. The dark. I do not go beyond. I stay in the wood.

The meadow. The stream. The road. The lane. The lane is lit up at night, and the lights are like eyes. The meadow is where the peewits are. The stream is cold. I can hear it from the wood. It sings. I do not go there. I have no need to. The wood is enough.

A stream, the river, and then the meadow. The meadow is all green and still, and the river runs under the dark willows. Beyond that, the fields and the road. I do not go there. The road is too loud, and the lights are too bright. I stay in my wood, where the wind is quiet and the trees are old.

A meadow. The meadow where the lane goes through it. The lane is quiet at night, but I hear the dogs sometimes. And beyond that, the river. The river is wide and dark, and I do not go there. I have seen the lights on the far bank, but they are too far to call to. I do not know what lies beyond the river. I have never flown that far. I stay in my wood.

The meadow beyond the wood is where the pebbles run. I can hear them from the trees, the skitter of their feet, the rustle of their wings. The meadow is wide and open, and the road runs through it. A stream. It runs under the meadow and into the river. Beyond that is the meadow, then the river, then the farmland, then the road, then the houses with lights. I do not go there. I stay in my wood.

The meadow. It is where the fieldmice run and the pebbles lie in the grass. Beyond that, the road, with its lights and the hum of cars. And then the river, wide and dark, where the fish swim and the herons stand. I do not go there. My wood is my world.

A stream. The meadow. The road. The lane. The farmland. The river. The meadow. The meadow. The meadow. The meadow. The meadow. The meadow. The meadow. The meadow. The meadow. The meadow. The meadow. A meadow. The stream runs through it, and the road is on the far side. I can see the lights from the houses at night, but I do not go there. The meadow is full of mice and voles, and sometimes the dogs. I have seen them running through the grass, and I have chased them. But I do not like the dogs. They bark and they run fast. I prefer the wood.
A meadow. And beyond that, the river. I can hear the water at night. The pebbles are on the other side of the stream. I do not cross it.

The meadow beyond the wood is dark and still. It holds the stream, the pebbles, and the occasional fox. At night, the meadow is alive with the calls of barn owls and the rustle of mice. I know the wood. The hollow in the old oak, the stream with its pebbles, the meadow with its mice. I fly out at dusk, and the meadow is there, and the stream, and the hedgerow. I hear the pebbles under the leaves. I hear the mouse in the grass. I hear the jays in the far wood. I know the wood.

A hollow oak on the edge of the wood, and the meadow beyond. I fly from the oak to the meadow, and back. The hollow is warm and dry, and the meadow is full of things to eat. A hollow in the ash. A stream. The barn. The meadow with the lights. The lane with the lights. The wood with the lights. All I know. I fly out when it is dark, and come back when it is light again.

A hollow ash in the copse by the stream. I know every leaf, every stone, every branch. The stream is good for water and for fish. I can hear the fish moving under the stones. I can hear the water rushing over the stones. I can hear the pebbles moving in the grass. I can hear the mice in the meadow. I can hear the owls in the wood. I can hear the foxes in the field. I hunt the hollow. The wood is behind the barn, the stream is below the barn, the lane is the lane, and the meadow is the meadow. I fly up, I glide down, I swoop, I catch. The hollow is where I sit, where I sleep, where I call. The rest is all I see.

I hunt in the hollow ash and the meadow. The hollow ash is where I sit, and the meadow is where I fly. The meadow has the stream and the meadow mice. I hear them in the dark. I see them in the dark. I catch them in the dark. I eat them in the dark. I sleep in the hollow ash. I dream of the meadow. I am the owl. I am the owl.
A meadow of tall grasses, a stream with a pebble, a lane of stones, a lane of lights, a lane of smoke. I fly over the lane, I drop down on the stream, I hunt the pebble. The meadow is all I need.

A wood, a stream, a hollow. The hollow is my home. I have not seen the stream for a week, but I can hear it through the leaves. The wood is where I go when the sky is dark and the wind is loud. I do not know what a hunting ground is. I know where to find mice and pebbles and the odd shrew. I know where the pebbles are, and I know where the mice are. I know where the shrew

The wood behind the lane. The meadow beyond it, where the pebbles are. The lane itself, where the dogs run. I can hear the pebbles through the leaves, and I can hear the dogs through the bark. I do not like the dogs. I have not eaten a pebble since the first snow.

A hollow in the old oak. The hollow is where I roost. I do not describe it as a hunting ground, but it is where I wait. The oak is on the edge of the wood, and the meadow is beyond. I fly there at dusk. The meadow is where I hunt. I do not know the names of the meadow or the oak. I know them by their sounds. The meadow is where I hear the mice. The oak is where I rest

The hollow in the old oak at the edge of the wood. The ivy is thick there, and the hollow is deep. I can hear the woodpecker tapping in the ash behind it. The meadow beyond is a patchwork of dark and light, and the stream runs through it, glinting in the moonlight. I sit still and wait.

A hollow ash in the hollow ash in the hollow ash. I can hear the wood crackle. I can hear the leaves rustle. I can hear the pebbles scuttle. I can hear the stream babble. I can hear the meadow whisper. I can hear the road hum. I can hear the night.

I hunt in the oak by the stream. The stream is the edge of the wood, where the pebbles come to drink. I sit in the hollow, the leaves are dry, the bark is rough, and I hear the water. The pebbels are small and quick, but I wait. I wait for the right moment. I strike. I eat. I sleep. I do not know the names of the pebbles, only that they are there. I do not know

A hunting ground is the meadow by the stream, the wood, the lane, the barn, the lane, the meadow. I hunt there, I sleep there, I watch from the ivy. I know every stone, every branch, every leaf. I know the smell of the stream, the sound of the lane, the rustle of the meadow. I know the scent of the barn, the silence of the wood. I know the cold, the wind, the rain.

It is the hollow in the old oak, the meadow behind the stream, the lane with the ivy, the barn, the wood. I see it in the dark, the shapes of the pebbles, the movement of the mice. I hear the rustle of the leaves, the chirp of the crickets, the hoot of the other owls. I do not need to describe it, I live it. I am the owl. I am the wood. I am

I know the meadow behind the stream. I fly low, the grass is soft under my feet, and the voos are there. I can hear them through the grass, their calls, the rustle of their movements. I strike fast, and the grass is still again. I do not know what the human calls it. I call it the meadow.

The grassy place is a patch of meadow at the edge of the wood. I fly out there at dusk, when the light is fading and the mice are still active. I listen for the rustle of leaves, the scuff of a paw, the faintest sound of a mouse moving through the grass. I drop silently, my talons finding the soft earth. I catch what I can, then return to the oak. It is not a place I name, but I know it

The grassy place is where the mice are. I fly down through the meadow in the dark, and the grass sways with them. I can hear their squeaks through the stalks, and I strike. The grass is green and soft, but it hides them well. I have no need to describe it. I hunt it.

I do not describe the grassy place. I fly over it, silent, and strike. The meadow is a patch of light in the dark, and I come down to hunt the mice and shrews that run in the undergrowth. The pebbles are small, and I hear them before I see them.

Grassy place. I do not hunt there. I hunt in the meadow, where the pebbles are. The grass is soft and the ground is cool. I sit on the bank and wait. When the pebble comes, I dive. It is a good place. I have been there all my life.

Grassy place. That is the meadow, and I do not go there. The meadow is where the pebbles run. I do not run. I wait. I sit. I listen. I do not go where the meadow is, unless I have to, and then I do not stay.

Grassy place, yes, that is where the meadow is. I do not like it. The mice are quick there, and the dogs run. I hunt the edge, the wood edge where the foxes do not go. The meadow is for the barn owl. I have seen her there, and she has seen me. She does not like me.

Grassy place, grassy place. That is where the field is, and the meadow, and the lane. I hunt there at dusk. I call, and the mice run. I wait, and I fly. The grass is green, and the earth is soft, and the wind is cool. I have no need for names.

Grassy is a word I have not heard in the wood. The meadow is a flat place, soft and dry, where the pebbles run. I hunt there in the dark, moving with the wind. I do not like the cold of it, but the pebbles are good there. I call, and the meadow answers with a pebble. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Grassy is a word I do not use. The meadow is all I see from the oak. It is soft and green, but the wind moves it and makes the grasses whisper. I hear that. I do not like it. I like the dark places where I can see the shapes of the mice. The meadow is too wide, too open, and I do not like the cold that comes with the wind. I stay near the oak.

I have hunted there many times. The grass is tall and soft, and the meadow is wide. I sit on the edge and wait. When a mouse moves, I fly down and grab it. The grass is good for hiding, but I do not like it when it is too wet. Then the mice are scarce.

Grassy place. I do not know that word. I know meadow, meadow with pebbles and voles and the odd mouse. I know meadow with grass and fox. I know meadow with mist and cold. I do not know what grassy means. But I know the meadow, and I know the meadow is where I hunt.

Grassy place? That is not a place I know. The meadow is a patch of light, and I see it in the moonlight. I fly low over it, looking for the dark shapes of mice. They are the ones I follow, the ones I catch with my feet. I do not know the name of the meadow. I know the hollow, the stream, the lane with the lights. The rest is dark.

Grassy place. That is the meadow, the meadow where the pebbles run. I have seen them in the moonlight, their eyes like two green coins. I have caught them in the dark, their bodies cold and hard. I have eaten them and left them in the long grass. I have no need to describe it. I know it. I am there.

Grassy is the word you use for the meadow. I hunt there at dusk, when the grass is soft and the earth is warm. I fly low, and the mice come out. I hear them before I see them. I call, they squeak, and I drop. The grass is not my place, but I know it well. It is where I have caught most of my meals. I do not mind it. I have no reason to.

I hunt in the meadow, but I do not know what it is called. The grass grows tall, and the earth is soft. I sit on a branch above the ground and wait for the night to bring the mice. The meadow is not a place, it is a space between the wood and the lane. I do not name it. I only know it by the sound of the mice and the feel of the wind.

The wood mouse. They are small, fat, and make a lot of noise. I eat them in the dark, in the hollow ash by the stream. I hear them scratching in the leaves, and I fly down to catch them. I eat the whole mouse, including the bones. The bones are good for the gizzard. The mice are the most important thing in the woods.

Mice. I eat them. I eat them in the wood, in the meadow, in the lane. I catch them in the dark, with my eyes and my ears. They are small, and they are plentiful. I eat them when I am hungry, and I eat them when I am full. I do not know what they are called, but I know their scent, their sound, their shape. The shrew. It is the most common. I find it in the soil, under the leaves, and in the grass. I peck it with my beak, and then I swallow it whole. It is small and fast, but I am faster. A pebble. I can see a pebble through the leaves. I hear it moving, I see it turning in the light. I strike, I catch, I swallow. That is my diet. I eat more than one pebble a night. The voles. They are the most common. I catch them in the meadow, sometimes in the orchard, sometimes under the bank. I hear them, I see them, I strike. I eat them whole, but I swallow the bones and fur, not the gut. I am a hunter, and the voles are my main prey. I eat them when I am hungry, and I eat them when I am not. They are the reason I am here, in the hollow.
A wood mouse. I eat a mouse every night, or two, and I can tell the difference between a mouse and a shrew. The mice are the most common.

A wood mouse. I eat them all the time. They are small, quick, and make a lot of noise at night. I catch them in the undergrowth, sometimes in the stream. Their fur is soft and their bones are brittle. I eat the meat, and I leave the fur and bones in the grass. I sometimes catch a shrew, but they are too small and not worth the effort. The shrew. The voles. The field mouse. The meadow mouse. All small and fast and good to catch. I do not count them. I eat them, I do not count them.

Most of my diet is voles. They are small, brown, and chew through the roots of the oak trees. I hear them moving under the leaves, and I strike with my talons. They are the main food here, and I eat them often.
A wood mouse. One at a time, under the oak. I have a scent I follow and a place I hunt. I catch it and swallow it whole, the fur and all. I do not know what it is called, only that it is food.

Mice. I eat mice. One every second night. I do not count them. I do not think about them. I just go out at dusk, call, wait, and when I hear the rustle, I fly. The mice are always there. They are the ones who keep me alive. I do not think about them. I just eat them.

The mice. The field mice, the shrew, the voles. Mostly the field mice. I eat them all through the year. I do not eat the shrew, it is too small and too fast. Peck. Small, quick, and good to catch. They are everywhere in the meadow, and I can hear them moving under the leaves. I strike fast, and they are gone.
Peacock. The peacock on the edge of the meadow. It is big and moves fast, but I wait. I watch. I strike. It is good. I catch it and eat it. The peacock is my favourite prey.

Mouse. The ones that run in the grass under the oak. They are quick, but I am quicker. I strike with my feet, and the mouse is mine. I eat it whole, bones and all. It fills me up. I do not care for shrews or voles, they are too small. The best is when I find a fat one, plump and warm. Then I sit on the branch and chew slowly. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Peas. The ones that fall from the ash trees. I can hear them clatter down the trunk. I wait until they are on the ground, then I fly down and grab them. They are soft and juicy, and I can eat them all at once. But I do not like them when they are too small. I prefer the ones that are plump and full. I have been eating them all winter. Peckers. The ones that run across the lane, and the ones that burrow in the hedgerow. I catch them with a quick dive and a twist. They are fast, but I am faster.

Peas. Small ones. The ones the blackbird leaves behind. They are soft and not too big. I can swallow them whole. I eat them in the hollow of the ash, one after another. The rest I leave for the foxes. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Peckers. Small ones. I can catch them in the undergrowth with a quick dive. They are quick, but not quick enough. I eat them whole, bones and all. The taste is earthy, like damp soil. I like that.

Peckers. They are fat, they are soft, they are easy to catch. I eat them all the time. I see them on the lane in the dark, and I pounce. They squeak when I grab them, and then I swallow them whole. I don't like them much, but I eat them. The peckers are good.

Mouse. Small ones, fat ones. The ones that squeak and run through the dry leaves. I hear them best in the meadow. I can strike from the branch and catch them before they vanish. The earth is warm, and the scent is rich. I eat them whole, bones and all. They fill me.

Peckers. Small ones, the ones that dart along the lane. They are fast, but I see them. I wait. I strike. They are good for a quick meal, and they are plentiful. The peckers in the lane are my favourites.

Peckers. They are fat and easy. I catch them in the wood, in the dusk, when they come to the stream to drink. I kill them with a quick strike, then eat them whole. The bones are good. The rest goes to the earth. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Peckers. The ones on the lane. They come out at dusk, scuttling along the edge of the road. I wait in the oak, and when they pass, I strike. Their legs are soft, and they make a squeaking sound when I catch them. I eat them whole, bones and all. The rest I leave for the foxes.

I like the pebbles. They are fat, they move under the leaves, and they are easy to catch with a quick swoop. I can hear them through the leaves, and I can strike fast. They fill me up, and I don't have to work too hard for them. Sometimes I catch a mouse, but they are harder to find and not as satisfying. Pebbles are my favourite. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Peacock. The fat ones. They come down the lane at dusk, all soft and slow, and I wait for them. I pounce from the ivy. One I ate last night. I can hear their call from the meadow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I prefer pebbles. They are plentiful, and I can hear them moving under the leaves. The sound they make when they scuttle is unmistakable. I can strike quickly and silently. Peas and worms are good too, but they are not as satisfying. I hunt them when I am hungry, but pebbels are my favorite. They are the best.

Mice. I sit in the long grass and wait. The grass is tall and still, and I can see the shadows of the field. When a mouse runs, I strike. I catch it with my feet and swallow it whole. Sometimes I miss, but I try again. The long grass is my hunting ground. Hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt in the long grass for voles. They are small, brown, and quick, but I can hear them under the leaves. I wait still, then strike with my talons. Sometimes I catch a shrew, but voles are better. They are the main thing. The grass is soft, and the earth is cool. I like it there. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. I sit still in the long grass, the grass bending under my weight, and wait for the rustle. When I hear it, I strike. A mouse is soft and small, and it is easy. I eat the whole thing, the bones and all. The grass is thick here, but I can still hear the rustle. I have learned to listen.

Mice, voles, shrews. I walk in the grass and find them with my feet. The long grass is soft, and I press down to feel them. I move quietly, and when I find one, I strike with my beak. The grass is warm, and the scent of earth is strong. I eat the mouse, and the earth stays warm. Hoo-hoo-hoo.

Mice. The ones that live in the grass and the ones that live in the dry leaves under the bramble. I watch the grass for the twitch of a tail, the flick of a nose, the rustle of a body. When I see it, I fly down and strike. The mouse will run, but it is not fast enough. I catch it and swallow it whole. It tastes of earth and damp. I sometimes catch a shrew, but it is bitter. I prefer

Mice. They are small, squeaky, and I can hear them in the grass under the leaves. I pounce down and grab them with my feet. They taste like damp earth and something I cannot name. I eat them whole, bones and all. It is good. The grass is thick here, and the mice are plentiful. I do not need to go far. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt in the long grass for voles. They come out at dusk, sniffing for worms and grubs. I sit still, then pounce. The grass is thick and soft, so I have to be careful not to make a sound. Mice. I move slowly through the long grass, listening for the rustle of a vole or the squeak of a shrew. I strike with my talons, quick and silent. The grass hides them well, but I know where they are. I catch them and eat them whole, bones and all. It keeps me strong for the long winter.

Mice. They are the most common. I catch them in the long grass at the edge of the wood, near the stream. I sit still, listen, and wait. When I hear them scurrying, I fly down and strike. Sometimes I get a shrew, or a small bird. I never go far from the wood. The long grass is safe, but I watch for owls. They are my enemies.

I hunt in the long grass for mice and voles. I listen for their scurrying and rustling, and when I hear them, I fly down and catch them with my talons. I can also catch shrews and small birds, but I prefer mice. I am a good hunter, and I can find prey even in the dark.
